section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Wave Nature of Light
section_1.content: Briefly review the principle of superposition and phase. Visualize light as a wave with crests and troughs, establishing that interference is the foundation for encoding information.
section_1.example: Visualizing two ripples in a pond colliding to create a complex interference pattern of peaks and valleys.

section_2.title: The Physics of Diffraction
section_2.content: Explain how light waves bend and spread around obstacles or through apertures. Introduce the Fresnel-Kirchhoff diffraction integral conceptually as the way light maps the 'shadow' of an object into a detailed interference pattern.
section_2.example: Laser light passing through a tiny pinhole expanding into a circular 'Airy disk' pattern on a screen.

section_3.title: Holography: Recording the Wavefront
section_3.content: Contrast photography (capturing intensity only) with holography (capturing phase and intensity). Show the 'reference beam' meeting the 'object beam' to lock the phase relationship onto a medium.
section_3.example: A futuristic 'Data Cube' device that captures the 3D position of a hummingbird by comparing a direct reference laser pulse with the light scattered off the bird's feathers.

section_4.title: Reconstruction: The Diffraction Reversal
section_4.content: Explain that the hologram acts as a complex diffraction grating. When a coherent light source illuminates the hologram, the stored interference pattern diffracts the light to recreate the original wavefront.
section_4.example: Using a simple smartphone flashlight behind a piece of holographic film to project a 3D image of a rotating gear into mid-air.

section_5.title: Summary and Real-world Application
section_5.content: Recap the sequence: Interference (recording) -> Diffraction (reconstruction). Connect this to modern technology such as heads-up displays (HUDs) or secure holographic ID markers.
section_5.example: A digital security tag that displays different depth-layered images of a guardian dragon when tilted under a light source.

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]

        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
